title: EEG Lempel-Ziv Complexity vis-à-vis Autocorrelation Function
authors: Pedro Montoya, Ignacio Cifre, José Luis Rosselló Sanz, Dante R. Chialvo
abstract: Measures of signal complexity have become increasingly popular in electroencephalography (EEG), where they are often interpreted as indicators of neural information processing, dynamical richness, or conscious state. In contrast, classical measures of temporal dependence, such as the autocorrelation function (ACF), remain more directly linked to known physiological mechanisms and are easier to interpret. The present work revisits, for the EEG practicioner, the relation between normalized Lempel-Ziv complexity (LZC) and temporal autocorrelation in both synthetic and physiological EEG signals. First, synthetic time series exhibiting a broad range of temporal structure and complexity levels were generated using stochastic processes with varying degrees of temporal dependence. LZC and autocorrelation measures were then computed and compared. Across simulated signals, a robust inverse relationship was observed between normalized LZC and the first autocorrelation coefficient, indicating that signals with stronger temporal correlations exhibit lower complexity estimates. This relationship also holds in resting-state EEG recordings from healthy adult participants across channels and subjects, as well as dynamically during eyes open/close maneuvers. Overall, these results show that the information captured by LZC reflects temporal redundancy already quantified by conventional autocorrelation measures. Because autocorrelation measures relate more directly to established neurophysiological mechanisms, including oscillatory persistence, network synchronization, and temporal integration, these results suggest that interpreting complexity-based EEG findings should explicitly account for their dependence on conventional temporal statistics, which may provide a more transparent framework for mechanistic inferences.
summary: This work compares Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC) against the Autocorrelation Function (ACF) using EEG data. The key finding is a systematic inverse relationship, indicating that LZC largely reflects temporal redundancy already captured by ACF. The authors recommend that complexity analyses must account for their dependence on basic temporal statistics for sound mechanistic inference.
main_problem: The paper revisits and compares the relationship between normalized Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC) and the Autocorrelation Function (ACF) in EEG signals to assess the interpretability of complexity measures.
main_result: A robust inverse relationship was found: signals with stronger temporal correlations (higher ACF) exhibit lower LZC. This suggests LZC captures information already quantified by conventional autocorrelation measures.
method: The authors computed LZC (using LZ76 on binarized signals) and ACF for both synthetic time series (from Markov chains) and physiological EEG recordings (resting-state and ERPs).
model_or_system: The primary system is Electroencephalography (EEG) signals, analyzed across synthetic time series generated by stochastic processes and real human data from resting-state recordings and evoked potential tasks.
key_observables: Normalized Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC), first-lag autocorrelation coefficient (AC1), and binary entropy rate.
important_parameters: The autocorrelation parameter ($ho$) used in generating synthetic Markov chains.
main_assumptions: LZC computation requires binarization of the continuous signal, and the authors caution that complexity measures aggregate multiple statistical properties whose mechanistic meaning is not straightforward.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate the systematic inverse relationship between AC and LZC for simulated Markov chains and confirm this relationship holds across different time windows and participants in real EEG data.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical comparison using synthetic Markov chains, demonstrating the inverse relationship. It then applies this analysis to real EEG data (ERPs and resting-state) to validate the finding across different physiological states.
why_interesting: While the subject is neuroscience, the rigorous comparison between two distinct measures of temporal structure (LZC vs. ACF) mirrors the methodological challenges in characterizing complex, non-equilibrium dynamics in physical systems.

FIG. 2: 1D random Cantor set: Autocorrelation (AC) and Lempel-Ziv complexity (LZC) relation computed numerically. The upper panel shows the Cantor set parameter P and the numerically computed lag-1 autocorrelation (AC1). The mid- dle panel compares the computed AC1 and the computed Lempel-Ziv complexity (plotted as 1 - LZC) across the range of ρ values. The lower panel depicts the weakly non-linear association between AC and LZC. As P increases, the cor- relation of the Cantor set increases, approaching a relatively more uniform (i.e., repeating) sequence, which is reflected as expected in the Lempel-Ziv complexity. Parameter b = 1/2. The data points are means and SDs from n=64 realizations.

FIG. 3: Progressive decimation of a correlated 1D random Cantor set: Autocorrelation (AC) and Lempel-Ziv complex- ity (LZC) relation computed numerically. The top two panels show LZC and AC1 as functions of increasing coarse-graining L. The bottom panel shows the same data as the top pan- els across the coarse-graining range. Notice the close corre- spondence between the two metrics as decimation proceeds, progressively decorrelating the random Cantor set. The data points are means and SDs from N = 64 stochastic realizations of the random Cantor set. Parameter values b = 1/2, P = 0.9 .
